ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: In the NMA tables and figures, participants are the number randomised to each treatment across its arms (NICE's N); elsewhere, N is the total number randomised in a trial or pairwise comparison.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> In the NMA tables and figures, participants are the number randomised to each treatment across its arms (NICE's N); elsewhere, N is the total number randomised in a trial or pairwise comparison.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("P = 0.64", "P = 0.56"), Sentence = c("Trials with an SSRI arm and no psychological therapy arm (22 of 23 rated high) against trials with a psychological therapy arm and no medication arm (32 of 36): Fisher's exact test, P = 0.64; restricting the SSRI group to SSRI versus pill placebo trials (12 of 12 rated high) gave P = 0.56.", "Trials with an SSRI arm and no psychological therapy arm (22 of 23 rated high) against trials with a psychological therapy arm and no medication arm (32 of 36): Fisher's exact test, P = 0.64; restricting the SSRI group to SSRI versus pill placebo trials (12 of 12 rated high) gave P = 0.56." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 108 columns across 12 data files.
#### Issues Identified

95 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 12 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

info.title: NICE's 2026 Consultation Draft Guideline for OCD and BDD (GID-NG10435): A Critical Appraisal with Secondary Analysis of NICE's Published Data
keywords: treatment resistance NICE OCD BDD Guideline Appraisal

author.affiliation:
Department of Neuropsychiatry
								National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery
								University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust

Deputy Chief Medical Officer
								Dalhousie University
								
									Cayman Islands Government
									George Town Halifax
									Nova Scotia
									Cayman Islands Canada

text.text: In September 2026 the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) opened consultation on the first batch of its update to the 2005 guideline for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) (GID-NG10435).
The draft replaces stepped care with matched care and reviews first-line treatment.

We appraised the draft and its supporting documents against six questions informed by selected AGREE II domains, analysing NICE's published effect estimates, sample sizes, sensitivity analyses and economic results descriptively; every value was checked against its source document.
Comparison guidelines were identified by a documented search.
The adult OCD review included 82 randomised controlled trials and the BDD review 13 studies.

The committee cited small samples and wide credible intervals when it did not recommend metacognitive therapy (52 participants) or eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR; 59 participants).

Self-administered cognitive behavioural therapy with therapist support, the second adult option, rests on 61 participants, with a wider credible interval than EMDR's, and was recommended on other documented grounds.
The top-ranked adult option had a probability of 0.17 of being the most costeffective.
The first-listed BDD option ranked fifth of nine in the network meta-analysis.
The draft gives no drug-specific dose targets, no consolidated definition of an adequate trial and no primary severity measure for allocation or response.

Treatment after non-response to an adequate trial is outside the scope of Batch 1; on the assumptions in NHS England's 2013 specification, a cascade beginning with 48 million adults in England and Wales yields approximately 48,000 people not responding to a serotonin reuptake inhibitor followed by local graduated exposure.
All six selected multimodal OCD comparison guidelines address augmentation; none provides a treatment pathway for BDD.
The draft rests on a substantial evidence synthesis.

The published rationale does not fully explain why small samples and imprecision precluded recommendations for some treatments but not others; several operational parameters are not specified; and further-line treatment is outside the first batch.
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) published its guideline on obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), CG31, in November 2005 [1].
text.formatted: The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) published its guideline on obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), CG31, in November 2005 <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: It was placed on NICE's static list in February 2014, and a surveillance review in 2019 concluded that it should be updated [2].
text.formatted: It was placed on NICE's static list in February 2014, and a surveillance review in 2019 concluded that it should be updated <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: NICE is updating the guideline in batches.
The draft scope, consulted on in May and June 2025, listed eight review questions, and the final scope, published in November 2025, retained four for the first batch [3, 4].
text.formatted: The draft scope, consulted on in May and June 2025, listed eight review questions, and the final scope, published in November 2025, retained four for the first batch <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4]</ref>.

text.text: The draft guideline for Batch 1 was published for consultation on 17 September 2026; consultation closes on 21 October 2026, and publication is expected on 16 February 2027 [5].
text.formatted: The draft guideline for Batch 1 was published for consultation on 17 September 2026; consultation closes on 21 October 2026, and publication is expected on 16 February 2027 <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: Under CG31, treatment was organised as stepped care, with intensity increasing in steps defined largely by functional impairment.
The draft replaces this with matched care, in which treatment is chosen at assessment according to the person's clinical needs, treatment history and preferences.
Its treatment tables for adults with OCD, children and young people with OCD, and people with BDD list options in an order "based on clinical-and cost-effectiveness evidence and safety" [6, p. 31].
text.formatted: Its treatment tables for adults with OCD, children and young people with OCD, and people with BDD list options in an order "based on clinical-and cost-effectiveness evidence and safety" <ref type="bibr">[6, p. 31]</ref>.

text.text: The evidence behind the tables comes from four evidence reviews, three network meta-analyses (NMAs) and three de novo economic models, all published with the draft [7] [8] [9] [10] [11] [12] [13].
text.formatted: The evidence behind the tables comes from four evidence reviews, three network meta-analyses (NMAs) and three de novo economic models, all published with the draft <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>.

text.text: This paper appraises the consultation draft and re-examines the quantitative results published with it.

It describes (1) what the update was intended to address and what Batch 1 covers; (2) the evidence base for each population; (3) how the documented reasoning links the evidence to the recommendations, and whether the documented reasons account for the differences between treatments; (4) how the draft handles combination treatment, dosing, treatment adequacy and assessment; (5) how its positions compare with contemporary international guidance; and (6) how many people may need treatment that is outside the scope of Batch 1, on the assumptions NHS England has published.
text.formatted: It describes <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref> what the update was intended to address and what Batch 1 covers; (2) the evidence base for each population; (3) how the documented reasoning links the evidence to the recommendations, and whether the documented reasons account for the differences between treatments; (4) how the draft handles combination treatment, dosing, treatment adequacy and assessment; <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref> how its positions compare with contemporary international guidance; and (6) how many people may need treatment that is outside the scope of Batch 1, on the assumptions NHS England has published.

text.text: Because the draft is open for consultation, its recommendations may change before publication.

We appraised the consultation draft [6], evidence reviews A to D [7] [8] [9] [10] and the technical appendices to evidence review B [14], economic analysis reports A to C [11] [12] [13], the draft and final scopes and NICE's responses to comments on the draft scope [3, 4, 15], health inequalities report A [16], the 2019 surveillance review [2] and CG31 [1].
text.formatted: We appraised the consultation draft <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>, evidence reviews A to D <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> and the technical appendices to evidence review B <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>, economic analysis reports A to C <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>, the draft and final scopes and NICE's responses to comments on the draft scope <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15]</ref>, health inequalities report A <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref>, the 2019 surveillance review <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> and CG31 <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: All were obtained from NICE's website between 17 September and 7 October 2026.
Population estimates were taken from NHS England's specification for the national service for severe OCD and BDD [17].
text.formatted: Population estimates were taken from NHS England's specification for the national service for severe OCD and BDD <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: AGREE II assesses clinical practice guidelines across six domains: scope and purpose, stakeholder involvement, rigour of development, clarity of presentation, applicability and editorial independence [18].
text.formatted: AGREE II assesses clinical practice guidelines across six domains: scope and purpose, stakeholder involvement, rigour of development, clarity of presentation, applicability and editorial independence <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref>.

text.text: This paper is not a formal AGREE II appraisal, which would require several independent raters and domain scores.

Six questions were informed by the domains most relevant to the content of the draft (scope and purpose, rigour of development, clarity of presentation and applicability): the purpose and scope of the update; the evidence base; the link between evidence and recommendations; combination treatment, dosing, treatment adequacy and assessment; consistency with international guidance; and the population outside the scope.
For each, we recorded what the draft and its supporting documents state, with page references, and compared the committee's documented reasons with the corresponding data.

Posterior median standardised mean differences (SMDs) with 95% credible intervals (CrIs), participants randomised, trial arms and median ranks were taken from the NMA tables of evidence reviews A to C; log-odds ratios for discontinuation for any reason, the results of sensitivity analyses and risk-of-bias ratings from the same reviews; net health benefit (NHB), quality-adjusted life years (QALYs), costs and probabilistic rankings from economic reports B and C; and prescribing and referral proportions from health inequalities report A [16].
text.formatted: Posterior median standardised mean differences (SMDs) with 95% credible intervals (CrIs), participants randomised, trial arms and median ranks were taken from the NMA tables of evidence reviews A to C; log-odds ratios for discontinuation for any reason, the results of sensitivity analyses and risk-of-bias ratings from the same reviews; net health benefit (NHB), quality-adjusted life years (QALYs), costs and probabilistic rankings from economic reports B and C; and prescribing and referral proportions from health inequalities report A <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref>.

text.text: Every row of each NICE results table used was transcribed, not only the rows discussed.
Values were extracted by one reviewer with AI assistance (see Acknowledgements) and were not double-extracted independently.

Instead, every transcribed value was checked by script against the text of its source PDF (the numbers in each row, in order), every quotation from a NICE or NHS England document was matched verbatim against its source, and every DOI was checked against Crossref.
The supplementary data give every value with its source table and page and the SHA-256 checksum of each source file [19].
text.formatted: The supplementary data give every value with its source table and page and the SHA-256 checksum of each source file <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: No new meta-analysis or economic modelling was performed, and no published estimate was re-weighted, pooled or adjusted.

The secondary analyses are descriptive: the width of each 95% CrI (upper minus lower limit); the change in each estimate between NICE's base case and its sensitivity analyses; NHB recalculated from the published QALYs and total costs as a check on extraction (all values agreed with the published figures to within 1 QALY per 1,000), and NHB differences expressed per person; mean participants per trial arm; the proportion of trials rated at high risk of bias by type of trial, compared with Fisher's exact test and a sensitivity analysis; and a recalculation, under alternative response rates, of NHS England's estimate of the number of adults who would not respond to a serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SRI) followed by local graduated exposure, with the specification's own rates as the reference case.

NHB is total QALYs minus total costs divided by the cost-effectiveness threshold of £20,000 per QALY; the models report it per 1,000 people over 12 weeks of treatment and five years of follow-up [12, 13].
text.formatted: NHB is total QALYs minus total costs divided by the cost-effectiveness threshold of £20,000 per QALY; the models report it per 1,000 people over 12 weeks of treatment and five years of follow-up <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13]</ref>.

text.text: Following NICE's usage, a difference is described as credible when its 95% CrI excludes zero.

Because an NMA estimate draws on direct and indirect evidence, its CrI, not the number of participants randomised to a treatment, is the measure of its precision; both are reported because the committee cited both.
Where NICE's documents give different values for the same quantity, both are reported, with the value used.
In the NMA tables and figures, participants are the number randomised to each treatment across its arms (NICE's N); elsewhere, N is the total number randomised in a trial or pairwise comparison.

Calculations were made in the workbook's formulas and checked against an independent calculation in Python 3.14, with Fisher's exact test from SciPy 1.18.1; each analysis, and every computed value reported here, is listed with its inputs in the supplementary data.

PubMed was searched on 30 September 2026 with the query ("Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder"[Mesh] OR "obsessive-compulsive"[tiab] OR "obsessive compulsive"[tiab]) AND ("Practice Guideline"[pt] OR "Guideline"[pt] OR guideline*[ti] OR consensus[ti]) AND ("2020/01/01"[dp] : "2026/09/30"[dp]).

Web searches combining "obsessivecompulsive disorder" and "clinical practice guideline" with "national", "society" and the names of countries were used to find national guidelines not indexed in PubMed.

Guidelines were included if they (1) made recommendations on the treatment of OCD in adults, either across treatment modalities or for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), deep brain stimulation (DBS) or ablative neurosurgery, the interventions covered by NICE's HealthTech guidance and the UK statement on neurosurgery; (2) were issued by a national or international professional society, government body or research consortium, with a stated method for grading evidence or recommendations; (3) were published between January 2020 and September 2026; and (4) were available to us in English, in full or as an official short version.
The restriction in criterion 1 to TMS, DBS and ablative neurosurgery was applied during screening and is stated here explicitly.

Two UK documents published before 2020 were included because they remain the most recent UK guidance in their fields: the British Association for Psychopharmacology (BAP) guidelines [20] and the Royal College of Psychiatrists' (RCPsych) statement on neurosurgery for mental disorder [21].

text.text: The PubMed search returned 46 records.
One reviewer screened titles and abstracts and checked the full texts of potentially eligible records; decisions and reasons for all 46 are listed in the data file.

Six records, describing five guidelines, met the criteria: the 2025 international guidelines of the Canadian Network for Mood and Anxiety Treatments and the International College of Obsessive-Compulsive Spectrum Disorders (CANMAT/ICOCS; [24]); the World Federation of Societies of Biological Psychiatry (WFSBP) guidelines, Version 3, Part II [25]; the Brazilian Research Consortium guidelines, Parts I and II [26, 27]; the Indian Psychiatric Society (IPS) 2025 update [28]; and the Congress of Neurological Surgeons (CNS) guideline on DBS [29].

text.text: No additional eligible guideline was identified by these searches.

The 2019 surveillance review gave, among its reasons for updating the guideline, "Advances in transcranial magnetic stimulation and deep brain stimulation technology for treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder" and the "Introduction of new pharmacological interventions and new augmentation therapies amongst treatment-resistant groups".

Stakeholders expressed concern at "a lack of provision for those individuals who remain treatment resistant at the end of the existing stepped care pathway as there are currently no recommendations covering this area", and described barriers in Improving Access to Psychological Therapies (IAPT, now NHS Talking Therapies) services that included significant waiting times, delays in referral and inaccessibility for some people "due to the severity of their OCD" [2].

text.text: Further-line treatment after no or limited response, including switching, augmentation and non-invasive neuromodulation, was listed among areas that may be covered in future batches, as was relapse prevention, which had not been a draft-scope question; recognition and assessment were moved to a separate guideline covering common mental health conditions.
NICE states that further updates will be decided once work on Batch 1 is complete [4].

text.text: In its responses to comments on the draft scope, NICE explained that all guidelines now have an 18-month maximum development timeline and that this, "combined with the volume and complexity of topics within the original scope", meant the guideline would be published in batches; it acknowledged that this was "a narrower scope than the consultation version" [15, pp. 1 and 3].

It answered 16 comments, including requests to define treatment-resistant OCD and to review augmentation, neuromodulation and ablative neurosurgery, by stating that further-line treatment or treatment-resistant OCD was no longer in the first batch (pp.
The draft sets out the limits of Batch 1 explicitly.
It does not cover further-line treatment after no or limited response, including switching and augmentation strategies, or relapse prevention [6, p. 1].

Its section on treatment notes that the committee did not review evidence specifically for people whose current episode has not responded to "at least 1 adequate trial (in terms of length, quality, and intensity or dose)" of a treatment option in the section, and states that "we cannot say whether the recommendations in this section are applicable to that population" (p. 30).
Where this population begins therefore depends on how an adequate trial is defined, which the draft does not consolidate (see 'Dosing and treatment adequacy').

Its update information states that it "is an update of NICE guideline CG31 (published November 2005) and will replace it" (p. 101), whereas NICE's project page states that the guidance "will partially update" CG31 [5].

text.text: The NMAs assume transitivity.

In the BDD network, NICE's estimates of the relative effects of active treatments were "based exclusively on indirect comparisons using waitlist as the common comparator" [9, p. 11]; a network of this shape has no closed loops, so the agreement between direct and indirect evidence cannot be checked.

text.text: The BDD economic model had no BDD-specific utility data: according to its parameter table, it took the utility of remission from adults with OCD and derived the loss of utility without remission from data on social anxiety disorder (the report's text assigns the two values the other way round; [13, pp. 21 and 44]), and it used OCD mortality risks.
The proportion of people with BDD receiving treatment came from a German study of 429 people with BDD, but other service use was estimated from data on adults with OCD [13, pp. 19-21 and 30].

text.text: The economic analyses report part of this uncertainty.

In the adult model, the probability that the top-ranked option, individual CBT, is the most cost-effective at £20,000 per QALY was 0.17, and the 95% intervals for the mean cost-effectiveness ranks were 1 to 8 for individual CBT, 1 to 10 for cognit-ive therapy and 1 to 8 for self-administered CBT with therapist support [12, Table 19, p. 61].

text.text: A threshold analysis found the preference for individual CBT or cognitive therapy (CT) over group CBT robust, although systematic bias across the whole network could not be ruled out, whereas placing self-administered CBT with therapist support above group CBT, the second and third options in the adult table, "was sensitive to small and plausible study level changes in the evidence" [8, p. 100].

For BDD, NICE's Technical Support Unit did not undertake a threshold analysis, because "there was no clear decision rule linking the recommendations on treatments for BDD to the respective BDD NMA results" [9, p. 11].

text.text: Behavioural therapy (BT) is not listed as a separate option; the committee noted that "CBT, CT, and BT are similar in clinical practice" [8, p. 99].

Metacognitive therapy (MCT) and eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR) receive no recommendation for or against: the draft lists options rather than recommending against the others, and the evidence review records the committee's reasons.
Serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) are likewise not listed.

text.text: The committee's documented reasons were as follows.

MCT was not included because the sample size was "relatively small (n=52 participants across 2 trials) with wide credible intervals", and "therapists should receive further training in order to deliver MCT".

EMDR had "only been tested on n=59 participants across 2 RCTs included in the NMA and reported wide credible intervals, which lowered the committee's confidence in the effect"; the committee discussed a possible benefit in trauma-related OCD, which the evidence did not allow it to analyse, and considered EMDR an area for future research [8, p. 101].

Self-administered CBT with therapist support was recommended because "there was a population who could benefit", including people who may not want group CBT and people with particular presentations of OCD such as scrupulosity, and after the committee considered the economic analysis (p. 99).

The draft's table describes its content as mirroring therapist-administered CBT protocols, so it shares its content with the first-listed option [6, p. 32]; the evidence review does not give this as a reason.

The committee also noted that the amount of support given in self-administered CBT could vary in practice and affect outcomes, and that lower levels of therapist support might be less effective [8, p. 99].
SNRIs showed no evidence of effect against pill placebo, and the committee "agreed that in practice these would also likely only be given as further line treatment".
SSRIs were recommended above clomipramine because of their precise estimate and their general tolerability and acceptability (p. 102).

text.text: Sample size.
Self-administered CBT with therapist support rests on 61 participants randomised to it in four arms, compared with 52 for MCT and 59 for EMDR.
In NICE's network for discontinuation the numbers are 67, 64 and 76 [8, Robustness.

In NICE's sensitivity analysis restricted to clinician-reported outcomes, the estimates for MCT and self-administered CBT with therapist support changed little (SMD -1.57 and -1.35, against -1.60 and -1.39 in the base case); neither was in the other two sensitivity analyses.

EMDR, with 30 participants in each sensitivity analysis, had similar estimates with comorbidities excluded and for clinician-reported outcomes (-1.37 and -1.38), and its interval crossed zero in the analysis restricted to first-line treatment, a network of four trials with waitlist as the reference (-1.18, 95% CrI -2.98 to 1.49; [8, Table 6, p. 71]).

text.text: Acceptability.

In NICE's NMA of discontinuation for any reason, which the review labels acceptability, the median ranks were 22 of 25 for self-administered CBT with therapist support (95% CrI 11 to 25), 8 for MCT (2 to 20), 13 for individual CBT (8 to 19) and 17 for EMDR (7 to 23), where lower ranks mean less discontinuation.
The log-odds ratios against pill placebo were 1.05 (95% CrI -0.32 to 2.45), -0.42 (-1.73 to 0.83), -0.01 (-0.92 to 0.89) and 0.31 (-0.52 to 1.16), all including zero [8, pp.
The comparisons between psychological therapies and medicines rest partly on indirect evidence, and trials of psychological therapy cannot blind participants to treatment.
These estimates therefore depend on the transitivity assumption (see 'Evidence base') and are more open to bias than their credible intervals alone indicate.

The committee also gave reasons other than sample size and precision, including the precision and tolerability of SSRIs and the training needed to deliver MCT; the draft does not state how these considerations were weighed against each other.

In NICE's pairwise analyses at six-month follow-up, with positive values favouring CBT, the SMD was 0.14 for CT (95% CI -0.13 to 0.42; score at follow-up; 2 RCTs, N = 209), 0.15 for MCT (95% CI -0.31 to 0.60; change from baseline; 1 RCT, N = 74) and 0.03 for EMDR (95% CI -0.50 to 0.56; score at follow-up; 1 RCT, N = 55; [35]); none of these differences was statistically significant.

text.text: At 12 months, NICE's analysis of one trial favoured CBT over CT (SMD 0.39, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.75; N = 119; [36]), although the trial report found no between-group difference in Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) score at any as-sessment point.

text.text: Non-significant differences do not establish equivalence, and NICE's pairwise comparisons were not non-inferiority analyses, although some of the trials were designed as non-inferiority trials.

text.text: The reported overall risk-of-bias ratings do not by themselves account for the different decisions.

NICE excluded no trial for risk of bias and rated 72 of the 82 included trials at high risk, for reasons that included incomplete reporting of allocation concealment and randomisation, missing data and the absence of a pre-specified protocol; the proportion was much the same for trials with an SSRI arm as for trials of psychological therapy (Table 4).

text.text: Self-administered CBT with therapist support rests on four arms of three small trials, two of them waitlist-controlled and all three rated at high risk of bias; of the two MCT trials, one [39] was among the ten not rated at high risk, and both EMDR trials were rated at high risk [8, pp. 16-60].

text.text: The ratings therefore favour neither medicines nor therapies, but nor do they separate stronger from weaker evidence.

What the review left out also matters: trials whose outcome data could not be extracted were excluded, among them three placebo-controlled SSRI trials with 846 participants between them and OCTET, a UK trial of supported self-help with 473 participants ([14, Appendix I]; sizes as stated in each trial report), so NICE's participant counts understate the evidence for both.

In the BDD economic model, group CBT had the highest NHB, with a probability of 0.74 of being the most cost-effective option, followed by self-administered CBT with therapist support, individual MCT and individual CBT, whose NHB exceeded that of waitlist by 8 QALYs per 1,000 adults [13, Table 15, p. 53].

text.text: The committee placed self-administered CBT with therapist support second, noting that some people with BDD find discussing appearance concerns face to face very daunting.

It placed group CBT below the other CBT formats because, although some people value the peer support of a group, many more find talking through body concerns in person and with several people very daunting, a point emphasised by committee members with lived experience; it added that group CBT might not suit people with severe functional impairment [9, pp.
The committee regarded discontinuation for any reason as "a proxy for treatment acceptability" (p. 43).

In the BDD NMA of that outcome, self-administered CBT with therapist support ranked last of six categories, with odds of discontinuation credibly higher than with waitlist (log-odds ratio 1.53, 95% CrI 0.21 to 3.13; three trials, 116 participants randomised); neither group CBT nor MCT was in the network [9, Table 6, p. 34].

The evidence for young people with BDD comprised one RCT with 30 participants in total, and the only BDD-specific SSRI trial in the review (fluoxetine, N = 67) was published more than 20 years before the 2026 draft.
Two independent meta-analyses found psychological treatment, mainly CBT, effective in reducing BDD symptoms: Liu et al.
[33] (15 RCTs, 905 participants) found robust evidence for that outcome but called for further research on others, and Zhao et al.
[46] (11 RCTs, 667 participants) concluded that more high-quality evidence is needed.

text.text: The draft uses the phrase "at least 1 adequate trial (in terms of length, quality, and intensity or dose)" to define the popu-lation it did not review (p. 30) but does not give a consolidated operational definition of an adequate trial.
Its guidance on duration appears in two places.

The SSRI row of the adult treatment table states that "Treatment should be continued for at least 12 weeks to evaluate response" and that "Benefits should be felt within 8 to 12 weeks" (pp. 33-34), while Recommendation 1.11.2 states that it can take "up to 12 weeks from reaching the maximum tolerable licensed dose" to see the full effects.

The table gives no starting point for its 12 weeks, whereas the 12 weeks in 1.11.2 run from reaching the maximum tolerable dose; the two coincide only if that dose is reached at the start, and the draft does not say which applies when judging whether a trial has been adequate.
The adult table also gives a usual course of 12 to 14 psychological treatment sessions, and the draft sets no threshold for response.

An international expert consensus defines response as a reduction of at least 35% in Y-BOCS score with a Clinical Global Impression-Improvement (CGI-I) rating of "much" or "very much improved", and partial response as a reduction of at least 25% but less than 35% with a CGI-I rating of at least "minimally improved", each lasting at least one week [49].

text.text: The draft mentions two validated instruments, the Obsessive Compulsive Inventory-Revised (OCI-R) and the Body Image Questionnaire (BIQ), and Recommendation 1.12.2 calls for "routine outcome monitoring with validated sessional outcome measures".
It does not name a primary severity measure for treatment allocation or for judging response, and the Y-BOCS is not mentioned in the recommendations.

Severity nonetheless informs treatment allocation: the draft defines the matched care approach as matching treatment to assessed clinical needs "such as symptom severity, degree of functional impairment" [6, p. 94], and its adult table describes self-administered CBT with therapist support as particularly suitable for OCD associated with less severe functional impairment, and both that format and group CBT as possibly unsuitable for OCD associated with severe functional impairment (pp. 32-33 and 36).
The draft does not define these levels.

text.text: Years in the column headings are guideline versions.

Of the six guidelines that cover several treatment modalities (CANMAT/ICOCS, WFSBP, BAP, Brazilian, German S3 and IPS), all six address augmentation after non-response to first-line treatment, which is outside the scope of Batch 1.

Adding an antipsychotic to an SSRI or clomipramine is the most consistent recommendation: CANMAT/ICOCS rates aripiprazole and risperidone first line in treatment-resistant OCD (Level 1); WFSBP grades aripiprazole, haloperidol or risperidone added to an SSRI LoE A, RG 2; BAP recommends considering antipsychotic augmentation [A]; the S3 guideline recommends aripiprazole or risperidone after at least 12 weeks of an SSRI or clomipramine, stopped after 6 weeks without response; and the Brazilian and IPS guidelines grade aripiprazole and risperidone with dose ranges.
Several also grade adding CBT with ERP after nonresponse to medication.

They differ on glutamatergic agents: CANMAT/ICOCS, BAP and IPS grade lamotrigine or memantine as options, whereas the Brazilian guidelines advise against routine use and the S3 guideline does not consider glutamate modulators indicated.
Four give drugspecific SSRI dose ranges; the BAP guidelines and the English short version of the S3 guideline advise increasing towards the maximum dose without stating ranges.
Five state a duration for judging a medication trial (WFSBP reports only the durations used in studies), and all six grade combined psychological and pharmacological treatment.

CANMAT/ICOCS offers a working definition of treatment resistance, the S3 guideline takes a reduction in symptoms of less than 25% as non-response, and the IPS guideline adopts the consensus definitions of response.
Cognitive therapy is rated first line by CANMAT/ICOCS and IPS.
MCT is third line in CANMAT/ICOCS and "may be considered" in the S3 guideline.
CANMAT/ICOCS is the only one to make a positive graded recommendation for EMDR (second line); WFSBP grades the evidence D, with no recommendation possible (RG 4).

Neuromodulation and neurosurgery are graded by fewer guidelines and come later in their sequences: repetitive TMS (rTMS) after non-response to earlier treatment, and DBS and ablative neurosurgery for severe illness that has not responded to several treatments.

For rTMS, CANMAT/ICOCS rates three adjunctive protocols first line in treatment-resistant OCD (Level 1) and the IPS guideline four (Level 2), WFSBP gives a limited recommendation and the S3 guideline states that it may be used after inadequate response, whereas NICE's HTG548 recommends TMS for OCD only in research [22].

text.text: To indicate the size of the population for whom further-line treatment is relevant, we used the illustrative cascade in NHS England's specification for the national service for severe OCD and BDD.

The specification estimates that about 1% of the 48 million adults in England and Wales, 480,000 people, may require treatment for OCD; that 60% respond to SRIs in primary care, leaving 192,000; and that 75% of these improve with graduated exposure delivered locally, so that "approximately 48,000 patients throughout the UK may be expected not to respond to treatment locally and require more specialised treatment".

Although the calculation starts from the adult population of England and Wales, the specification describes the resulting 48,000 as patients "throughout the UK"; the figures in this section refer to adults in England and Wales.

The specification adds that augmentation "may be effective in up to 50% patients", which "would leave 24,000 patients still needing further treatment"; if fewer respond, more remain ( [17]; Figure 4).
text.formatted: The specification adds that augmentation "may be effective in up to 50% patients", which "would leave 24,000 patients still needing further treatment"; if fewer respond, more remain ( <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref>).

text.text: The specification notes that "only a small percentage of sufferers present for treatment", so these figures describe need rather than demand.
The calculation is sequential: it applies the response rate for graduated exposure in general (75%) to people who have not responded to an SRI, and the specification gives no rate for that group.

text.text: NICE's own analysis of primary care records gives a more recent view of treatment.

Among adults with a recorded diagnosis of OCD or BDD in the three years before 1 February 2025, 16% of men and 14% of women had been prescribed an antipsychotic in the preceding three months, against 52% and 53% prescribed an SSRI; 11% of each had been referred to NHS Talking Therapies [16, pp. 8 and 26-27].
text.formatted: Among adults with a recorded diagnosis of OCD or BDD in the three years before 1 February 2025, 16% of men and 14% of women had been prescribed an antipsychotic in the preceding three months, against 52% and 53% prescribed an SSRI; 11% of each had been referred to NHS Talking Therapies <ref type="bibr">[16, pp. 8 and 26-27]</ref>.

text.text: The report cautions that "the data do not capture treatment indication or sequencing", and it reads the rise in antipsychotic prescribing with age as "suggesting greater clinical severity or complexity in older populations" (pp. 2 and 25).
Adding an antipsychotic is the augmentation strategy that the comparison guidelines recommend most consistently (see 'Comparison with international guidance'); Batch 1 does not address it.
The draft rests on a substantial synthesis: four evidence reviews, three NMAs and three economic models, with 82 RCTs for adult OCD.
Its leading recommendations for adults broadly correspond to the NMA and economic rankings, although NICE's own probabilistic and threshold analyses show substantial uncertainty in the ordering.
Five further findings emerge from the published data.

First, the reasons documented for not recommending MCT and EMDR, small samples and wide credible intervals, also describe self-ad-ministered CBT with therapist support, which was recommended on other documented grounds.
Second, the ordering of the BDD treatment table differs from both the BDD NMA ranking and the ranking in the BDD economic model.
Third, the draft does not specify drug-specific dose targets, a consolidated definition of an adequate trial, a response threshold or a primary severity measure.
Fourth, treatment after non-response to an adequate trial is outside the scope of Batch 1, and the draft marks none of CG31's recommendations as retained.

On the assumptions of NHS England's 2013 specification, a cascade that begins with 48 million adults in England and Wales leaves approximately 48,000 people not responding to an SRI followed by local graduated exposure; if those two treatments are regarded as adequate trials, these people are one subgroup of the population outside the scope of Batch 1.

Fifth, on augmentation, dose ranges, neuromodulation and neurosurgery, the positions of the draft and of NICE's HealthTech guidance differ from those of most comparison guidelines, and the NICE draft is the only guideline in this comparison set with a treatment pathway for BDD.
NICE committees weigh clinical effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, feasibility, equality and experience, and the reasons recorded in the evidence reviews may not capture every consideration.
This appraisal compares only the documented reasons with the published data.

Sample size and credible-interval width are not decision rules in NICE's methods; they are compared here because the committee gave them as reasons for not including MCT and EMDR, and the comparison shows only that these reasons do not by themselves separate the options that were included from those that were not.

Where the same stated criterion applies to options that received different decisions, the difference may reflect other considerations, such as the training needed to deliver a therapy, the theoretical overlap between CBT and CT, the value of a low-intensity option, or the acceptability of a format, which the committee cited for group CBT in BDD; the documents do not set out how these were weighed.

The draft notes that the higher placing of individual therapist-administered CBT and CT may increase the use of psychological therapies, which "could impact service capacity and workforce planning" [6, p. 39]; the training needed to deliver MCT was among the committee's reasons for not including it [8, p. 101].

text.text: The treatment tables are ordered lists.
Where more than one option is appropriate, recommendation 1.9.4 asks clinicians to "offer the appropriate treatments in the order listed" [6, pp. 30-31].
text.formatted: Where more than one option is appropriate, recommendation 1.9.4 asks clinicians to "offer the appropriate treatments in the order listed" <ref type="bibr">[6, pp. 30-31]</ref>.

text.text: The economic model gives the top-ranked adult option a probability of 0.17 of being the most cost-effective, and NICE's threshold analysis found the order of the second and third adult options sensitive to small changes in the evidence, although it found the preference for individual CBT or CT over group CBT robust, so the ordering carries more uncertainty than an ordered list conveys.

For BDD, the committee departed from a small and poorly connected network, and NICE's Technical Support Unit judged a threshold analysis infeasible because no decision rule linked the recommendations to the NMA.
Phased development is common in guideline updates.
The consequences of phasing here depend on the final guideline: the draft states that it will replace CG31, while the final scope allowed recommendations to be retained.

If CG31's recommendations on poor response are not carried forward, NICE guidance will not address treatment after first-line non-response unless a later batch covers it; if they are carried forward, they will not have been reviewed since 2005.
The differences from international guidance partly reflect different remits and evidence thresholds; on augmentation, they reflect the scope of Batch 1, which excluded it.
NICE assesses neuromodulation and neurosurgery through a separate HealthTech programme, and its guideline methods give weight to cost-effectiveness and to the certainty of evidence.
Several comparison guidelines grade treatments on smaller or uncontrolled bodies of evidence, and some make recommendations for settings with different licensing, costs and resources.

This appraisal uses only documents in the public domain, reports every extracted value with its source table and page, and provides the extracted data, calculations, an analysis register, checksums of the source files and the guideline screening decisions as supplementary data.
It also has limitations.
It is not a formal AGREE II appraisal: there was no independent rating or domain scoring.
Values were extracted, and search records screened, by one reviewer with AI assistance, without independent double extraction or screening.
Script-based checks against the source documents reduce, but do not remove, the risk of transcription error, and they cannot detect an error in a source document.

The appraisal questions and analyses were not preregistered; to limit selective reporting, every row of each NICE results table used was transcribed, and the comparisons were chosen to test the reasons the committee documented.

The secondary analyses use NICE's published summary estimates; they cannot account for correlations between estimates or re-run the NMA, and CrI width is a descriptive measure of precision rather than a test.
We did not obtain the executable economic models, which NICE supplies on request, subject to a signed confid-entiality agreement.

The NHB values, costs and probabilistic ranks are therefore NICE's published results: the appraisal could not test the models' assumptions, re-run their probabilistic analyses or examine other scenarios, and the recalculation of NHB checks only that the published figures are internally consistent.
NHB differences expressed per person describe model output at £20,000 per QALY over the models' time horizon, not health gained by individual patients.
Without the BDD model, we could not establish whether the report's text or its parameter table correctly describes the sources of the utility values (see 'Evidence base').
The economic model for children and young people (economic report A) was not analysed.
The recalculation of NHS England's estimate uses illustrative response rates and, like the specification, assumes that the rates apply in sequence.

The guideline search was restricted to Englishlanguage documents found through PubMed and web searches, which excluded two Dutch consensus statements and a French practical guide and may have missed other national guidance; the ISRS guideline on radiosurgical capsulotomy was not included because its full text was not available to us.

One eligibility criterion, the restriction of single-intervention guidance to TMS, DBS and ablative neurosurgery, was clarified during screening rather than prespecified; it excluded one record, on transcranial direct current stimulation.
HT has interests relevant to treatment after first-line non-response, which are declared below.
The draft may change after consultation; this appraisal describes it as published for consultation.
NICE's consultation draft for OCD and BDD moves from stepped to matched care on the basis of a substantial evidence synthesis.

The published rationale does not fully explain why small samples and imprecision precluded recommendations for some treatments but not others; NICE's own analyses show that the ranking of options is uncertain; and several operational parameters, including dose targets, a consolidated definition of an adequate trial and a primary severity measure, are not specified.

Treatment after non-response to an adequate trial, which includes the neuromodulation and augmentation approaches cited in the 2019 surveillance review, is outside Batch 1, and with no CG31 recommendation marked as retained, guidance for this group in the interim is unresolved.
On several questions, including augmentation, dose ranges, neuromodulation and neurosurgery, its positions differ from those of most contemporary international guidelines.
